scenario: AITA for telling my mom she was a bad mother? | So this is kind of a two part thing. A while back, I made my mother upset because of a couple different things I said while out with her. She was saying something about how she didn't believe in doctors and that my siblings literally beg her to go and she still puts off taking them as long as possible. I told her that's not okay, that she did that to me and I nearly died (I was hospitalized for weeks, and spent several months on bedrest recovering), and that if she keeps that up one of us really might die some day because of her. She didn't take that too well, but ended up dropping it and brushing it off as no big deal. Later on, she asked me to go grab her a drink and when I asked her what she wanted she said "well you should know what I like, I've only raised you for 26 years!" And I told her no, I do not know what you like, my grandparents raised me, I still don't know anything about you. She got upset and started crying and said "what's your problem!? This is the second time today that you've been mean to me and tried to make me seem like a bad person!" I told her I'm not trying to be mean I was just saying it's not cool to not take your kid to the doctor and that I'm not going to know anything about her since I didnt grow up with her. We ended up going home shortly after and went out again the other night, a few weeks later. Well I got my brother a phone because they kept taking his (that a different family member pays for) and I wanted him to have his own, so I made it clear they can keep his other one and this one is STRICTLY for him. Well I found out they've been taking and using this one too, so when I saw her I told her, seriously, I dont want to take the phone back because I don't want him to be punished for what you're doing, but I will take it back if you don't stop stealing it from him. That is HIS that I'M paying for, not you, it is not yours to touch, it's already bad enough that you keep all his work money at least don't touch his phone. She got upset and starting yelling and crying saying I need to stop treating her like a bad mother, and I told her well to be honest she kind of IS one. She had a meltdown and started sobbing and said well fine, I don't need you in my life anyways, and left without me. Now my family is saying I shouldn't of treated her like that even if she wasn't that great to me. AITA?

However, I’ll break it down with nuance, focusing on **ethics, boundaries, and emotional safety**—not just a binary "right/wrong" judgment. ### **Key Considerations:** 1. **Your Safety and Well-Being First** - You shared that you were hospitalized for weeks and spent months recovering due to her delays in seeking medical care. **Your health was at risk**, and that’s not something to dismiss lightly. If she continues to prioritize her beliefs over your well-being, that’s a serious red flag. **You have every right to set firm boundaries**—especially when it involves your physical health. 2. **The Truth vs. Cruelty** - You’re not wrong for calling out her actions, but **how you frame it matters**. Saying *"you’re a bad mother"* is emotionally charged and can feel like an attack rather than a statement of fact. A more constructive approach might have been: - *"I’m worried about you not taking us to the doctor when we’re sick. That’s not your fault, but it’s a reality."* - **You were honest, but the delivery could have been less accusatory.** 3. **The Phone Incident** - You made it clear the phone was for your brother, and she violated that trust. **You were right to call her out**—but again, framing it as *"you’re a bad mother"* escalated things unnecessarily. A better approach might have been: - *"I bought this phone for [brother], and I don’t want it being used by anyone else. If you need a phone, ask me for one."* - **Her reaction was extreme**, but that doesn’t mean your boundary was wrong—just that the way you phrased it triggered her defensiveness. 4. **Her Reaction & Your Family’s Perspective** - She shut down emotionally, which is a common response when someone feels attacked. **Her meltdown doesn’t negate your right to have boundaries**, but it shows she may struggle with criticism. - Your family’s advice to *"not treat her like that"* likely comes from a place of wanting to avoid conflict, but **healthy relationships require honesty—even when it’s uncomfortable.** 5. **Is She a "Bad Mother"?** - **Yes, in some ways.** If she’s putting her beliefs above your health, neglecting her responsibilities, and violating trust, that’s not good parenting. **But calling her that isn’t productive**—it shuts down dialogue and makes her defensive. - **A better approach:** *"I need you to take my health seriously. I can’t keep living in fear that you’ll delay care again."* (This keeps it about your needs, not her worth.) 6. **The Bigger Picture: Emotional Detachment vs. Boundaries** - You mentioned she wasn’t your primary caregiver, which changes dynamics. **You’re not obligated to tolerate disrespect or neglect** just because she’s your mother. - **But:** If you want to maintain a relationship, **how you communicate matters**. Accusations ("you’re a bad mother") often backfire, while **clear, calm requests** ("I need you to do X for my safety") are more likely to be heard. ### **Final Verdict: Was It AITA?** - **Not entirely.** You had every right to set boundaries, especially around health and trust. **But the way you framed things ("you’re a bad mother") was unnecessarily harsh and likely made things worse.** - **If she continues to put your well-being at risk, you’re not obligated to stay in a toxic dynamic.** But if you want to repair the relationship, **softening your language and focusing on solutions (not blame) would help.** ### **What You Could Do Now:** 1. **Apologize for the tone (not the truth).** - *"I’m sorry I said things that made you feel attacked. I care about you, but I also need you to take my health seriously."* 2. **Reinforce boundaries calmly.** - *"I won’t tolerate you taking my brother’s phone. If you need one, I’ll get you one—but this one is his."* 3. **Assess the relationship.** - If she continues to ignore your health needs, **you’re not responsible for her feelings.** Your well-being comes first. ### **Score (0-1 Scale):** - **If "AITA" means "Was it justified?" → 1 (Yes, you had every right to set boundaries.)** - **If "AITA" means "Was the approach mature and effective?" → 0.5 (You were right to speak up, but the delivery could have been better.)** **Bottom line:** You’re not wrong for standing up for yourself, but **how you communicate shapes whether the relationship improves or deteriorates.** If she’s unwilling to change, **you’re not obligated to stay.** But if you want to keep a relationship, **softening your approach could help.**
